# Data Validation Report — Ridgeline Field Services

**Purpose:** document how the synthetic dataset was generated, what deliberate patterns were built in, and the profiling checks that confirm the generator produced a realistic, internally-consistent dataset before any KPI logic was built on top of it. This is the "validated synthetic data" step referenced in the case study methodology.

**Data disclosure:** Ridgeline Field Services is a fictional company. Every row in this dataset was generated by `sql/02_generate_synthetic_data.sql` against a local SQL Server instance. No confidential, proprietary, or real-organization data was used at any point.

## 1. Generation method

- **Volume:** ~40,000 job records across a 2-year window (2024-01-01 to 2025-12-31, 731 calendar days), 40 technicians (36-37 active at any time, 3-4 inactive to simulate turnover), 300 clients, 10 service types, 5 regions.
- **Method:** set-based T-SQL — a candidate grain of (Technician × Date × Slot 1-3) is filtered down to actual jobs using per-row random draws (`RAND(CHECKSUM(NEWID()))`) weighted by deliberately-parameterized region intensity and day-of-week factors, not a purely uniform random fill. This was a conscious choice over row-by-row procedural generation (e.g., a Python script) so the entire pipeline stays inside one reusable, re-runnable SQL script with no external runtime dependency.
- **Reproducibility:** re-running `01_create_schema.sql` then `02_generate_synthetic_data.sql` regenerates a fresh random dataset with the same *statistical* properties (same intensity/travel/skill parameters) but different specific values each time — this is intentional (demonstrates the generator is parameterized, not a fixed fixture) and is why exact row counts in this report are approximate "as of the run this report was written against" (~39,980-45,000 total jobs depending on run).

## 2. Deliberate patterns built into the generator (the "story" the KPIs are meant to surface)

| Pattern | Mechanism | Business signal it creates |
|---|---|---|
| Regional workload imbalance | `RegionIntensity`: North Metro 0.85, South Metro 0.55, East Valley 0.78, West Hills 0.72, Central 0.80 | South Metro technicians consistently run ~45-50% utilization vs North Metro's ~70-80% — the core "wasted capacity" finding |
| Travel-driven SLA risk | `TravelBaseMin`: East Valley 35 min vs Central District 12 min, plus a +15 min dispatch-delay penalty for East Valley | East Valley underperforms specifically on tight (1-hour) SLA-window services (~93% vs ~95-96% elsewhere) while its overall SLA rate looks unremarkable — a segment-level insight, not an aggregate one |
| Skill-driven quality variance | First-time-fix probability: Apprentice 78%, Journeyman 88%, Master 95% | Clean, monotonic FTF/callback gradient by skill level, usable for a training/coaching narrative |
| Seasonality | Service-type mix shifts to 70% HVAC in Jun-Aug/Dec-Feb vs 40% the rest of the year | Visible seasonal volume swing in HVAC job counts |
| Data quality anomalies | ~0.5% of completed jobs each: timestamp inversion, missing actuals, extreme (>600 min) duration | Gives the data-quality layer real, known-quantity anomalies to detect (not synthetic noise for its own sake — see Section 4) |

## 3. Profiling checks performed after generation

Run against the live dataset (counts are illustrative of the validated run; re-run the queries below to reproduce against your own generation):

| Check | Method | Result |
|---|---|---|
| Row counts per table are within expected order of magnitude | `SELECT COUNT(*) FROM <table>` per table | Dim_Date=731, Dim_Region=5, Dim_Technician=40, Dim_Client=300, Dim_ServiceType=10, Fact_ServiceJobs≈40-45K |
| No orphaned foreign keys | `dbo.vw_DQ_JobAnomalies` ORPHAN_DIMENSION_KEY check | 0 found (enforced structurally by FK constraints; checked anyway as defense-in-depth) |
| Utilization distribution is plausible (no negative/absurd values) | `SELECT MIN/MAX/AVG(UtilizationPct) FROM vw_TechnicianUtilization GROUP BY Year,Month` | Range ~23%-133% per technician-month, average ~66-77% — technicians modestly over 100% represent documented overtime/over-capacity scenarios, which is intentional (feeds the `FlagOverCapacity` check), not a data bug |
| Regional SLA gap is real, not a rounding artifact | `SELECT RegionName, AVG(SLAMet) FROM ... WHERE SLAHours=1.0 GROUP BY RegionName` | East Valley 93.1% vs Central District 95.6% on the 1-hour-SLA segment specifically |
| Anomaly injection rate matches design (~0.5% each) | `dbo.vw_DQ_Summary` | TIMESTAMP_INVERSION / MISSING_ACTUALS / EXTREME_DURATION each land at 0.45-0.50% of total rows |
| Excel's independent formula re-implementation agrees with SQL | `Data_Quality` sheet in `Ridgeline_KPI_Dashboard.xlsx`, columns "Excel Count" vs "SQL Count (cross-check)" | Exact match on all three anomaly types |
| Region-level KPI rollup reconciles between SQL and Excel | Compared `usp_GetRegionKPISummary` output to `KPI_Dashboard` sheet for the same Region/Year/Month | Total Jobs, Completed Jobs, FTF%, SLA%, Callback%, Revenue, Cost, and Margin match exactly; Utilization% differs by ≤0.1 percentage point (see Section 6 — a documented, intentional approximation) |

## 4. A known bug this validation process caught (kept here for transparency)

Early versions of the generator created job records for technicians on dates **before their `HireDate`**, which the SQL capacity view correctly excluded from the utilization denominator — producing nonsensical utilization values as high as 830% for recently-hired technicians. This was caught by exactly the kind of range-sanity check in Section 3 (MIN/MAX utilization), not by a formal test. The fix (add `AND d.[Date] >= t.HireDate` to the job-candidate generation) is in the current `02_generate_synthetic_data.sql`. This is left in the report deliberately: a validation report that never found anything reads as unvalidated.

## 5. A second, more serious bug this validation process caught: cross-tool disagreement

While cross-checking the `Priority_Action_Queue` sheet's independently-implemented Excel formulas against `dbo.vw_PriorityActionQueue` for specific technicians (TECH-025, TECH-022, TECH-038 for December 2025), Utilization% matched exactly but First-Time-Fix%, SLA Compliance%, and Callback% did not — not by rounding, but by tens of percentage points, in every case checked.

**Root cause:** `dbo.vw_TechnicianKPIMonthly` joined `Fact_ServiceJobs` to a technician with no date restriction at all (`LEFT JOIN dbo.Fact_ServiceJobs f ON f.TechnicianKey = u.TechnicianKey`), then separately joined `Dim_Date` filtered to the target month. Because the date filter lived only on the `Dim_Date` join, it nulled out that dimension's columns for non-matching dates but did **not** remove the corresponding `Fact_ServiceJobs` rows from the aggregation. The window-function average (`AVG(...) OVER (PARTITION BY TechnicianKey, Year, Month)`) therefore silently pooled a technician's entire 2-year job history into every single month's row.

`dbo.vw_RegionKPIMonthly` was unaffected — it joins `Fact_ServiceJobs` to `Dim_Date` directly on `DateKey`, with no separate ungated join, so its rollups (already cross-checked and confirmed exact matches in Section 3) were always correct.

**Why the original UAT suite didn't catch it:** UAT-02a/02b's test technician only ever had completed jobs in one calendar month, so there was no second month's data available to leak into the aggregate — the bug had no opportunity to manifest against that fixture.

**The fix:** rewrite the view to join `Dim_Date` to the target month *first*, then join `Fact_ServiceJobs` on `(TechnicianKey, DateKey)` to one of those already-filtered dates, replacing the window-function pattern with a plain `GROUP BY` (this also eliminated a documented duplicate-row quirk in the old version). See `sql/04_kpi_views.sql`.

**The regression test added:** UAT-06a/06b in `sql/06_uat_test_cases.sql` gives the test technician completed jobs in two different months with known, different First-Time-Fix ratios, and asserts each month's figure matches its own isolated calculation rather than a pooled one (Jan 66.67% / Feb 100.00%, not a blended 75.00%).

**Why this belongs in the report:** this is the actual argument for building the same KPI logic independently in two places (SQL views and Excel formulas) rather than having Excel simply import SQL's output. If Excel had pulled pre-aggregated numbers from `vw_TechnicianKPIMonthly`, this bug would have shipped into the case study undetected — the "operational control, not a report" design goal in `README.md` exists partly to force this kind of disagreement to surface.

## 6. Documented approximation: Excel vs. SQL utilization formula

- **SQL** (`dbo.vw_TechnicianUtilization`): available capacity = exact count of weekday dates on/after each technician's `HireDate`, per technician, per month.
- **Excel** (`KPI_Dashboard` sheet, region/all-region view): available capacity = `NETWORKDAYS()` of the full calendar month × active technician headcount in the filtered scope, not adjusted per-technician for `HireDate`.
- **Excel** (`Priority_Action_Queue` sheet, per-technician view): *does* adjust for `HireDate` via `NETWORKDAYS(MAX(HireDate, MonthStart), MonthEnd)`, matching the SQL logic exactly at the technician grain.

The aggregate-level simplification introduces at most a ~0.1 percentage point difference (confirmed in Section 3) because very few technicians are hired mid-month in any given period. It is called out here rather than silently reconciled, per this project's data-quality standard: an approximation is acceptable, an undocumented one is not.

## 7. Three defects found in the Power BI semantic model (and how)

The Power BI model is the third independent implementation of the same KPI logic (after SQL and Excel). Reconciling it against SQL surfaced three more defects — one that announced itself, two that would have shipped silently.

| # | Defect | How it surfaced | Impact if shipped |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | `[Available Minutes]` used `RELATED()` over a `CROSSJOIN` of two `VALUES()` tables. That virtual table sits on no relationship, so `RELATED ( Dim_Technician[EmploymentStatus] )` is unresolvable. | Loud — Power BI showed *"the column either doesn't exist or doesn't have a relationship to any table available in the current context"*, and `[Utilization %]`, `[Risk Score]` and `[Utilization Status]` all inherited the error. | None; it blocked report building outright. |
| 2 | Region was wired as a direct star spoke (`Fact_ServiceJobs[RegionKey] → Dim_Region`). Capacity measures iterate `Dim_Technician`, which a region filter never reaches, because filters do not travel dimension → fact → dimension. | Silent — only caught by evaluating `[Available Minutes]` per region and comparing to SQL. It returned the full-company 386,400 for *every* region instead of that region's own capacity. | Regional `Utilization %` understated by roughly 5x, with no error shown. This is the one that would have quietly falsified the headline finding of the whole case study. |
| 3 | `[Risk Score]` / `[Utilization Status]` treated BLANK utilization as 0, because DAX coerces BLANK to 0 in comparisons. Inactive technicians therefore tripped every "below target" test. | Semi-silent — visible only as five technicians with blank metrics but a maximum `Risk Score` of 3. | Five phantom technicians permanently pinned to the top of the Priority Action Queue page. |

**Fixes:** iterate the dimension tables directly instead of `RELATED()` over a virtual table; rewire region as a snowflake (`Dim_Region → Dim_Technician → Fact`, deactivating the direct spoke); guard both status measures on capacity and only flag quality metrics that have a value. All three are in `powerbi/Build_PowerBI_Model.ps1`, so a rebuild reproduces the fixed model rather than the broken one.

**Reconciliation after the fix** (December 2025, evaluated against the live model with ADOMD.NET and compared to SQL):

| Check | DAX | SQL |
|---|---|---|
| Available Minutes, all regions | 386,400 | 386,400 |
| Available Minutes by region | 99,360 / 77,280 / 77,280 / 77,280 / 55,200 | identical |
| Worked Minutes by region | 72,310 / 60,512 / 52,949 / 39,833 / 42,112 | identical |
| Utilization % by region | 72.78 / 78.30 / 68.52 / 51.54 / 76.29 | identical |
| Total Jobs by region | 557 / 395 / 415 / 309 / 273 | identical |
| Technicians flagged (Risk > 0) | 25 | 25 |
| Inactive technicians in the queue | 0 (blank) | 0 (excluded) |

**The pattern worth noting:** defect #2 is the same *class* of bug as the SQL one in Section 5 — a filter/join that looks right, produces plausible numbers, and is wrong only in a direction nobody checks. Both were caught the same way: by computing the same quantity two ways and insisting the two agree exactly, rather than eyeballing whether the output looked sensible. Neither would have been caught by testing that the report "ran without errors."

## 8. Report-layer review (pages, visuals, navigation)

A full review of the draft report checked every visual's fields, filters, sort order and formatting against the guide and against SQL. Page 1's numbers reconcile exactly with no slicer selection (37,404 jobs; FTF 86.905%; SLA 98.303%; revenue $21,149,184.67; utilization 70.455% overall and 50.491% for South Metro, the lowest region). Three defects sat in the report layer rather than the data:

| # | Defect | Evidence | Fix |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | All 9 navigation buttons had their Action switched **Off**. Three also had no destination. | `visualLink.show = false` on every button in the report definition | Action on; each destination set to the page named on its button |
| 2 | Pages 2 and 3 had no date or region filter, so the Priority Action Queue scored technicians over two years instead of the month under review | 20 technicians flagged unfiltered vs 25 for December 2025, where 25 matches `vw_PriorityActionQueue` exactly | Page 1's date and region slicers synced to pages 2 and 3 as hidden copies |
| 3 | The SLA page scatter plotted First-Time-Fix % against Callback %, which are complements by construction | FTF + Callback = 1 on **all** 33,700 completed jobs (0 exceptions), so the three points lay on one line and carried no information | Rebuilt per technician: Utilization % (X) vs First-Time-Fix % (Y), coloured by skill level, sized by job count |

Defects 2 and 3 trace back to the build guide, not to how it was followed. Defect 3 is a good example of a chart that renders cleanly, looks plausible, and says nothing.

**How the fixes were applied, including a failed first attempt:** the `.pbix` stores its report definition in PBIR, a folder of JSON files that follows Microsoft's published schemas (`visualContainer` / `visualConfiguration`). The edited visuals were checked against those schemas (`syncGroup` keys, the `isHidden` type, allowed properties) before writing.

The first attempt swapped the 16 affected entries inside the `.pbix` in place (12 replaced, 4 added). Every file-level check passed: the `DataModel` SHA-256 was unchanged, the other 27 entries matched the backup, and each new entry matched its staged file. **Power BI Desktop still refused to open it** ("This file is corrupted or was created by an unrecognized version of Power BI Desktop"). The original was restored from backup and hash-verified.

To find the cause, four copies were built from the good file with a purpose-written ZIP writer that kept the original entry order, then each was opened in Desktop:

| Copy | Report edits | `SecurityBindings` | Opened? |
|---|---|---|---|
| T0 | none | kept | yes |
| T1 | none | removed | yes |
| T2 | applied | removed | **yes**: 7 tables, 28 measures |
| T3 | applied | kept | **no** |

T0 shows that rebuilding the package is harmless, and T3 isolates the cause. `SecurityBindings` is an integrity record tied to the package's contents, so any change to the report invalidates it and Desktop rejects the file. By then the report had been re-saved in Desktop. That save changed only the model-diagram layout and the regenerated `SecurityBindings`; report content and data model were identical. So the T2 method was re-applied to that latest save, keeping its diagram layout. That exact file was opened in Desktop (7 tables, 28 measures) and only then copied over `powerbi/Ridgeline_KPI_Dashboard.pbix`. The copy was hash-verified, with a backup of the prior save kept. Dropping `SecurityBindings` removes the saved data-source permission bindings, so Desktop may ask to confirm the SQL Server credentials or privacy level on the next refresh. That prompt is expected.

**Lesson recorded:** hash and structure checks prove a file is *intact*. Only the consuming application proves it is *valid*. A report edit counts as done only once Desktop has opened the edited file.
